members.title: 《深空当铺》1.0版修改器：玩法拓展|添加物品|背包整理

news.body:
深空当铺在28号发布正式版更新，相信超长内容的demo版本大家也是玩法非常上头，在这个更新之际也给大家盘点了一下几个非常值得装的mod，不光是demo版本还是之后的正式版中，都分别进行了功能适配，完美符合包括只玩demo以及购入正式版体验的朋友，大家有需要可以安装下~
首先是修改器内容，我这里用到的是xmod，不光支持正式版以及demo版，并且支持修改器+mod进行整合，（工具可以浏览器下载，下载后主页优惠兑换输入【鸭鸭】获取时长）目前支持的功能有：
游戏速度调节
设置店铺吸引力
增加信用点
这里重磅介绍下物品添加面板：打开后可以选择你需要的任何物品，点击后即可一键添加到背包：包括所有的货物、装备武器、物资设施、消耗品、以及特殊物品
选中后输入你想要的数量即可~
当然如果你感觉修改器只是数值上的编辑，想要更多内容上的拓展，也可以直接使用xmod内部的mod功能，这里推荐几个超级好用的mod，并且包含安装！
本次mod推荐提供mod整合好后一键安装的方法！
一键安装方法如下：浏览器搜索xmod进入官网，下载后主页输入【鸭鸭】获取时长~直接在xmod内深空当铺页面的mod广场里面选择想要的mod即可一键安装！
好了正式开始mod介绍：
1、背包整理：
详细描述：
物品整理功能让你在界面上一点即可清理存储空间。打开任意存储容器时，会出现一个小窗口，里面有一个整理按钮。按下按钮后，里面散落的物品会被整齐紧凑地重新排列。物品会按大小分组，并在有助于放入时自动旋转，让你无需手动拖拽就能获得更多可用空间。已放置的存储单元（如隔间和笼子）被视为固定家具，因此整理存储时只会在它们周围重新排列散落物品，绝不会移动这些单元本身。
2、检查助手：
详细描述：
在你检查物品或接待顾客时自动弹出信息窗口，把游戏内部已经算好的鉴定结果直接呈现出来。四个功能均可独立开关——右键放大镜即可打开设置界面。
主要功能：
真伪鉴定助手用放大镜检查注射器、香烟、食品券时，自动显示 5 项检测目标，有问题的项目标红，正常的标绿。
价值鉴定：鉴定可估价物品（如肋排三明治、等离子燃料匣等）时，显示鉴定委员会认定的真实价值。
改造体警告来访顾客是改造体时立即弹出警告，并根据普通/困难模式提示“击杀后改造体灭绝”或“放走后数量超阈值”等后果。
通缉犯警告：来访顾客是通缉犯时显示其真实姓名和举报奖励金额。
一键设置：右键放大镜即可打开设置界面，随时开关上述四个功能。
3、酿酒扩展
详细描述：
这个模组为赛博城市带来了8种全新作物、8种水果和8种酿造酒，还有一台瓶子打印机！
扩展存储
详细描述：
本 Mod 为玩家提供一个原版风格的额外仓库，复用游戏原生库存网格、物品拖拽、物品形状占格、堆叠、边界检查、窗口和存档系统。
以上是我感觉必装的几个mod,其他推荐mod：物品拓展包、自动备份、水塔、霰弹枪、更多食物以及钓鱼等等大家可以根据自己需求安装~
我这里用到的mod都已经整合在了xmod工具内，浏览器搜索xmod进入官网，下载后主页输入【鸭鸭】获取时长~直接在xmod内深空当铺页面的mod广场里面选择想要的mod即可一键安装！
大家可以在这里挑选所有自己喜欢的mod,工具内集成了上百种mod，当然如果你有玩其他游戏，这里也可以使用其他游戏~
记得输入【鸭鸭】哦！

news.title: 《恶魔城》新作玩砸了，“恶魔城Like”还有戏吗？
news.summary_raw: 《恶魔城：贝尔蒙多的诅咒》口碑两极遭遇大量差评，分析其翻车核心原因，同时以《银松镇》为例，探讨“恶魔城Like”品类的发展潜力。

members.title: 《恶魔城》新作玩砸了，“恶魔城Like”还有戏吗？

news.body:
看到“媒体好评如潮”与“玩家骂声如潮”无缝汇作一体，我们就知道，《恶魔城》这次，真的玩砸了。
自从2026年10月15日，《恶魔城：贝尔蒙多的诅咒》上架Steam以来，这款带着“阔别多年的恶魔城IP正统续作”光环登场的B级游戏——定价才￥128，显然不是什么3A大作——就为我们呈现出了一派彻底分裂的口碑：
打开metacritic搂一眼就知道，一方面，以IGN为代表的媒体给这款作品打出了80分以上的好评，但在另一方面，Steam平台超过5500条留言中好评率只有76%——倘若把语种切换成中文，那么超过1000条评论当中只有35%给予了肯定——由此一来，《恶魔城：贝尔蒙多的诅咒》这番开门算不算成功，相信诸位心中自有结论。
不难想象，此番风评一出，“恶魔城作为IP这次属实凶多吉少”的言论立刻开始甚嚣尘上——不过，排除无意义的跟风起哄不提，作为近30年来最受欢迎的商业游戏类别之一，时至今日，“恶魔城Like”留给我们的生命力以及发掘潜力，究竟还有多少呢？
先别急着下定论，这是个远比预想中更有趣也更有料的话题。
并非外行
首先需要明确一点，尽管争议之声此起彼伏，但《恶魔城：贝尔蒙多的诅咒》并不是什么外包给外行糊弄玩家的不可燃数字废弃物：
在这款作品的“开发者”一栏，我们可以很清楚地看到除了KONAMI之外还有一家名叫Evil Empire Studio的制作组，相信大多数见多识广的朋友立刻就能反应过来：没错，这就是那家著名另类小众（并不是形容词）独立游戏开发组Motion Twin的“同位素”制作组，而Motion Twin最近一次在主流玩家群体中引发震动的大新闻，是这个：
没错，著名小众（？）Roguelite/银河恶魔城Like游戏《Dead Cells》的《恶魔城》DLC。
虽然在名义上仅仅是借用了知名IP声望拓展开发的补充包，但这款DLC在玩家社区引发的震荡不仅大大出乎Motion Twin的预想，就连KONAMI也没预料到居然会有那么多的《恶魔城》玩家慷慨解囊纷纷买账——有了这个大获成功的合作先例，继续发扬光大为《恶魔城》系列继续制作正统续作，就某些意义而言似乎也不是说不过去——于是，就有了现如今的《恶魔城：贝尔蒙多的诅咒》。
由此可见，尽管在游戏行业的打拼资历确实和KONAMI这种老资格没法比，但对于Evil Empire Studio来说，长线运营维护定期更新《Dead Cells》这种显而易见受到“银河恶魔城”启发而来的游戏，至少在“专业性”层面上还是很有保障的；事实上，如果屏蔽社区舆论重新打开《恶魔城：贝尔蒙多的诅咒》，至少在动作系统方面的打击感、流畅度乃至开局上手操作体验方面还是可圈可点的，排除一部分兼容性引发的游戏启动问题不说，至少在第一印象上《恶魔城：贝尔蒙多的诅咒》表现还是合格的——所以，现如今这番层出不穷的差评印象，又是从何而来的？
答案并不神秘：
当Evil Empire Studio（或者说Motion Twin）的调性，遇上了一碗水端不平的“恶魔城”系列新作，这种风评结局几乎是必然的。
熟悉《Dead Cells》的朋友都知道，一方面，作为一款以“横板跳跃/探索随机地图过关”为核心的Roguelite游戏，Motion Twin和Evil Empire Studio确实尽最大努力实现了“多种类型的玩家都能找到各自的乐趣”这个设计目标——无论是玩弹反的ACT爱好者，还是不拼反应单靠策略过关的RPG拥趸，至少在理论上，都可以从这款作品当中找到符合自己胃口的玩法。
但在另一方面，不同的玩法究竟能不能收获同样愉悦的游戏体验，那恐怕就得多上个问号了——以完全不依赖反应的Roguelite/RPG玩家为例，虽然我们可以找到很多远程武器乃至“释放后不管”的自动炮台来进行攻关，但从中期开始，这套玩法的疲态就逐渐开始浮出水面，即便算上Roguelite的局外成长资源要素，挫折感十足的半路翻车也是家常便饭，再加上《Dead Cells》在这方面的成长曲线并没有想象中那么流畅（攒下许多资源去解锁完全背离使用习惯的武器装备，显然不是人人都能接受的，偏偏《Dead Cells》就有这类内容），“新手上路属实好玩”与“耐玩度较之Roguelite老牌劲旅依旧有差距”的印象，已然大成。
OK，理解了Evil Empire Studio的基本调性，再让我们回头看看《恶魔城：贝尔蒙多的诅咒》，“褒贬不一”乃至“多半差评”的反馈，完完全全属于理所当然：
熟悉“恶魔城”这个IP的朋友都清楚，作为发展至今已有40年的化石级经典系列，“恶魔城”大致可以划分为ACT驱动的“经典恶魔城”，以及RPG驱动的“银河恶魔城”；而就在这两者之间的分界线上，赫然是一座影响力至今都未曾散尽的巅峰之作——
《恶魔城：月下夜想曲》。
作为彻底改变了整个系列潮流走向、进而对整个游戏产业尤其是独立游戏行业造成过巨大影响的划时代杰作，《恶魔城：月下夜想曲》值得探讨的亮点实在是不胜枚举，但如果放在今天这个主题框架下，咱们需要关注的只有一点：
——为什么《恶魔城：月下夜想曲》如此出色？
——盖因这款作品给予了我们真正的“自由选择”。
一方面，对于完全不擅长ACT的朋友来说，《恶魔城：月下夜想曲》包含一整套成长路径清晰无比的角色培养系统，只要按部就班地刷经验攒钱收集道具，通关完全没有任何困难——包括隐藏关在内，无伤干掉所有Boss（包括隐藏Boss），全然没有任何难度。
没错，这款游戏的RPG要素就是这么圆满，之所以时隔30年依旧有无数人将《恶魔城：月下夜想曲》视作整个系列的制高点，原因无他，“第一款不靠修改开挂，单凭认真体验就能打出完美结局的恶魔城”，足以说明一切。
而在另一方面，对于那些习惯了传统恶魔城紧张刺激ACT体验的朋友来说，《恶魔城：月下夜想曲》同样包括一整套碗大量足的动作游戏系统——并不是什么“调剂口味搞那么一两个场景解解馋”，而是整张地图都可以通过原汁原味的“经典恶魔城”模式体验下来，再考虑到作为32位主机的PlayStation性能要比之前的8位机16位机强太多，与大幅增强的画面表现力同步飙升的ACT模式主角实力，属实让习惯了经典恶魔城滋味的朋友在找回熟悉的感觉之余，对“技术进步”的实际意义产生最直观的认知。
——而这对于正在开疆拓土的Sony来说又意味着什么，恐怕已经不需要任何解释了，没错，天时地利人和，正是《恶魔城：月下夜想曲》真正的魅力根源所在。
也正因如此，《恶魔城：贝尔蒙多的诅咒》之所以会遭遇这么多非议，答案一目了然：
“这体验的自由度甚至还不如《Dead Cells》，我玩它作甚？”
对于时隔这么多年依旧对“恶魔城”这个IP不离不弃的玩家来说，“心满意足”的上限固然很高，但“值得尝试”的下限，也并没有想象中那么苛刻：尽管在经验、档期、预算上限以及产品定位等因素的驱使下，《恶魔城：贝尔蒙多的诅咒》的完成度与打磨精细度注定不可能达到《恶魔城：月下夜想曲》的程度；但即便如此，倘若集中成本在“满足玩家需求多样性”这个议题上尽量做到最好，如今的抱怨声还会有那么高吗？
答案我们心中自然有数。
《恶魔城：贝尔蒙多的诅咒》翻车了，这点毋庸置疑——不过，倘若就此判定“恶魔城Like”就此一蹶不振再无出头之日，——那倒也未必：
让我们再来看看《银松镇》。
当《寂静岭》《生化危机》遇上《恶魔城》……
“……？”
——我相信，但凡是从PlayStation和SS一路走来的老玩家，看到这个章节的标题，脑海中的直觉反应100%会是一个“大惑不解”：
“这几个当年包机房最热门的经典，怎么就融合到一起了？”
——一点没错。尽管听上去属实离谱，但这就是《银松镇》，2026年秋季档“银河恶魔城Like”赛道上最瞩目的选手之一：
再考虑到这款作品是几个大厂老兵正式组队之后鼓捣出来的第一步作品，“好评如潮”的含金量有多高，我相信大多数正在向着这个目标冲刺的朋友再清楚不过——OK，那么从实际体验的角度出发，《银松镇》到底有什么好玩的？
答案很简单——这款作品，是近年来为数不多在真正意义上实现了“高概念经典游戏要素无缝融合”的代表作：
举个例子，经典的《生化危机》是如何营造恐怖感的？答案是资源管理——从武器弹药的数量到药物补给的分布，再到物品栏格子的多寡，攸关“续航”的每一项要素都被明确限定了规模，而这也正是《银松镇》所呈现的重点：捉襟见肘必须对携带物品进行取舍的背包格子，极其有限的武器耐久度，再加上可以组合特定道具节约携带空间的“融合”设计，旧时代《生化危机》那些耳熟能详的要素，在《银松镇》当中真就是一个都没落下，甚至包括“存档必须消耗特定道具”这个噱头也不例外——总之，对于久经沙场的老玩家来说，《银松镇》攸关游戏性的第一印象，完全可以达到11/10的程度。
其次，如果单从操作性和机动能力一类的综合性能来看，《银松镇》的主角几乎是近年来具备动作要素的新游戏当中，实际表现最差的那一档——听上去不是什么好事，但对于熟悉经典惊悚冒险游戏的朋友来说，第一时间想到的多半是《寂静岭2》当中那个同样毫无ACT天赋的主角；没错，无论是战斗力简直就是个笑话的操控角色，还是四处雾气弥漫的场景环境，抑或是扭曲到近乎失去人形的敌方怪物，再加上语焉不详需要玩家自主拼凑的“这究竟是个什么故事”，《银松镇》攸关感性体验的要素，完完全全就是照搬了全盛期的《寂静岭》引人入胜的那一套——尽管在表现力上有所不同，但对于真正有经验的老玩家来说，给个10+2/10的评分丝毫不算意外。
再者，对于经典的“银河恶魔城Like”游戏来说，“不能从这一侧打开”的门户，以及必须通过特定手段开启的通路，是约束调整玩家攻关次序的核心要素，而在《银松镇》当中，这些设计同样也没有缺席，甚至还有了全新的进步：
在不少“银河恶魔城Like”游戏当中，“拿到了新能力，却想不起能用在哪些机关上”属实是个让人头大的问题，对于那些只能通过碎片时间忙里偷闲的玩家来说尤为严重，而《银松镇》选择了一个极其直接的方法近乎完美地解决了这个麻烦：利用游戏内置的相机，我们可以直接给场景中“需要以后再来解锁”的机关拍张照片（还可以缩放镜头来呈现重点），然后直接将这张照片作为附件添加在游戏内置的大地图上，从性质到位置一目了然，轻而易举就能唤醒我们的回忆——不得不说，从设计理念来说显然不是什么“前无古人”的创意，但对于“银河恶魔城Like”来说实用性如何，我相信，但凡有过那么一点实际体验的朋友，都不可能给这个设计打低分。
综上所述，从项目构成的角度来看，《银松镇》完全不是什么开创了行业先河的新理念新制作——事实上，除了前面提到的这三个典型学习范本，见多识广的朋友还能在这部游戏当中看到更多耳熟能详的要素，包括《Splatterhouse》《Another World》乃至《双峰》，可谓是见识越广对这款游戏的评价就越高——而对于“银河恶魔城”这个类别来说，这种“海纳百川，取其精华”的创作思路，永远是这个赛道上不可动摇的核心理念之一：
融合的魅力
正如“银河恶魔城Like”这个Tag所示，自从在20世纪90年代起，吸纳融合了《超级银河战士》的构成要素之后，“恶魔城”这个IP才得以跨越时代一路发展到今天；换句话来说，从这个转折点算起，“捡进碗里都是菜”就是这个品类不可动摇的构成理念之一，既然如此，现如今的我们，为什么不来继续沿着这个思路试试看呢？
举个最简单的例子：错综复杂、环环相扣的场景设计，是不少《恶魔城》作品当中引人入胜的一环，许多优秀的场景单凭布局以及BGM就足以让无数玩家流连忘返，那么，如果能将这些场景不仅仅视作跑图的背景板，而是进一步开拓修葺成为让我们休息调整的基地，又会是种什么体验呢？
再进一步的话，理所当然，这种“鸠占鹊巢”的操作，势必会引来“原生势力”进行反扑，倘若需要我们一次次回城手动打退进攻自然是对游戏节奏的极大破坏，但换个思路，假如让我们结合箱庭地形，为营地安装各种自动迎击的炮塔设备和陷阱机关呢？假如这些陷阱机关不仅支持自由DIY，更能作为探索隐藏房间的战利品，从大地图的各个角落里直接拆解、搜集随后化为己用呢？
没错，大多数朋友肯定都能看出来，这种“据点建设+自动化塔防”的玩法属实不是什么新鲜事儿，但对于“银河恶魔城Like”来说，既然从一开始核心受众就没有排斥过“取百家之长”的游戏构成方案——换言之，只要能与箱庭探索的内核巧妙咬合，那么“应缝尽缝”不仅不是缺点，反而能擦出意想不到的火花。
正所谓办法总比困难多，只要打开思路进行探索，“恶魔城Like”值得发掘的潜力，远比我们的预想来得更广——《恶魔城：贝尔蒙多的诅咒》翻车带来的失利，或许反而为我们腾出了破旧立新的契机。先别灰心，让我们再来试试看吧。

news.body:
"Developers need to treat Early Access like a real launch, because players do" – Early Access games are on the rise, but so are player expectations
The studios behind Valheim, Subnautica, Hades, Phasmophobia, Paralives, and Deadhaus Sonata discuss the highs and lows of Early Access
The number of games released through Steam's Early Access program has risen significantly in recent years. According to SteamDB, 2,924 Early Access games launched on Valve's platform in 2026 (as of mid-October), an 18% increase from 2025 and a 60% increase from 2020.
As a percentage of the overall number of Steam games released each year, Early Access titles are on the rise, going from a 10.4% share in 2024 to 11.3% in 2025 and 13.7% in 2026.
When Steam launched its Early Access program in 2013, it opened a valuable door for solo developers and smaller studios, allowing them to raise capital mid-development while simultaneously building hype and gathering vital player feedback ahead of a 1.0 launch. Don't Starve, Baldur's Gate 3, and Dead Cells are just some examples of how a constructive Early Access period can lead to long-term success.
But rather than simply buying time to tinker, a game's Early Access launch is now just as important as its "real" launch. GameDiscoverCo reported that only 21% of Steam Early Access graduates earned more in their first 30 days after 1.0 than after their Early Access release.
GamesIndustry.biz spoke to the studios behind Valheim, Subnautica, Hades, Phasmophobia, Paralives, and Deadhaus Sonata about the rising bar for Early Access releases, the benefits and pitfalls of gathering player feedback, and the things they would have done differently.
The quality bar rises
Nowadays, when it comes to Early Access, absolutely anything goes, says Anthony Gallegos, creative director of Subnautica 2. "It's not a few edge-case games participating anymore," he tells GamesIndustry.biz. "Early access could mean a game like ours doing long-term open development, or it could be a game three months from a 1.0 release that's effectively doing a paid beta soft launch and using the Early Access term as a way to soften player expectations."
All in all, that makes for a "more diverse and confusing landscape," he says.
One thing is certain though: competition in the Early Access space is higher than ever. Daniel Knight, CEO and game director at Phasmophobia maker Kinetic Games, says that whether Early Access or 1.0, new releases need to be at "a much higher quality." Paralives developer Alex Massé says he ended up delaying the game's Early Access launch from December 2025 to May 2026 after pre-release tests revealed the tutorials and some other features weren't up to scratch.
Richard Svensson, CEO of Valheim developer Iron Gate, believes that player expectations for an Early Access game are about 20% lower than for a full release, but they are still high. "They might be more forgiving when it comes to content, but they still expect a polished game."
However, for Denis Dyack, CEO of Deadhaus Sonata developer Apocalypse Studios, a key factor that's making the landscape more challenging is that anyone, including "giant publishers with insane amounts of money, manpower, and resources," can launch a game into Early Access.
"They can put up a polished product and rake in cash; it's a marketing beat for them," he explains. "So, that leaves players often expecting a near-perfect game that, in our opinion, defeats the purpose of Early Access, which is a collaborative development process based on player feedback. AAA publishers are abusing Early Access, skewing player expectations in such a way that it heavily disadvantages smaller independent developers." He cites Subnautica 2 and Path of Exile as examples of Early Access games "drastically changing the landscape and players' expectations."
Dyack explains that Apocalypse Studios never expected Deadhaus Sonata to be compared to Early Access games with AAA budgets and, as a result, says the team hit "significant barriers to entry" and had their marketplace impact "significantly reduced."
"Smaller teams are being held to a much higher standard than they were in the past"
"Players naturally compare everything in the same marketplace, so smaller teams are being held to a much higher standard than they were in the past," adds Ethan McKinnon, creative director at Apocalypse Studios.
Both McKinnon and Dyack advise developers entering Early Access to keep this in mind, recommending they also prioritise strong game performance (and an understandable concept), take Steam reviews into account, and build trust with influencers to go toe-to-toe with AAA marketing budgets. "Developers need to treat Early Access like a real launch, because players do," McKinnon says.
Key to success
Early Access has been an incredible boon for a number of developers. "If Early Access as a model hadn't existed, Valheim never would have gotten as big as it did," says Iron Gate CEO Richard Svensson. "Even if we had an enormous budget and worked on the game in secret for five years up until the launch, we never would have been able to reach the amount of people that we have."
"Having the game out there and being able to work with the live community is really the only way that Valheim would have ever reached the success it has."
Subnautica is another game that benefited massively from the initiative. "When the first Subnautica entered Early Access, it was a new program for Steam, with no real process or understanding of what did and didn't work," recalls Gallegos (the game launched in December 2014, the year after the program started). "The team viewed it as an opportunity to experiment with content and features alongside players in real time." The experiment paid off in both financial and development terms, with player feedback being instrumental in shaping the game's direction.
So when it came to deciding whether Subnautica 2 should launch in Early Access, there was "no decision to make," Gallegos says. "Participating in Early Access means we can still pivot and change the game in meaningful ways that simply launching a complete experience and hoping we got it right wouldn't allow," Gallegos explains. "It's core to our DNA now."
Greg Kasavin, creative director at Supergiant Games, is also a convert. "Early Access development was instrumental to the success of the original Hades, inspiring us to make a bigger and better game than we would have otherwise," he says. "So we knew we wanted to reapproach that process with Hades 2."
The opportunity to gain some much needed funding is one of the big draws of Early Access. After starting the quirky life-sim Paralives as a solo project in 2019, Massé used funds raised through Patreon to put together a studio to develop it, but he still faces a Goliath. Paralives' main competitor, The Sims 4, boasts over 12 years of content and the financial backing of EA.
According to Massé, for Paralives to offer the same amount of content and features, a "ton of work" is needed. So he launched Paralives into Early Access in May 2026 – and within eight hours, it had sold 250,000 copies. "As a small team and because of the scope of the game, Early Access was the only option," Massé says. "[It] gave us financial security and allowed us to collect a huge amount of feedback that we can use to improve the game."
The game changer
Direct feedback from your target audience is another key draw of Early Access. "Communicate openly with your players," advises Gallegos. "Be honest with them and make them understand how crucial they are to the process. Preserve your vision, but listen to them and let them help you bring the best out of your game."
Svensson echoes this sentiment. "You need to remember that it's about working with a community. If you don't want to do that, you might as well develop your game on your own and release it once it's done," he says. "However, you need to make sure that you still have a clear vision for the game you want to make; otherwise, you risk getting run over by the community completely."
To butcher an old saying, no plan survives contact with the players. But it's still important to have one. "Go into it with a plan," advises Knight. "But also be willing to change the plan."
It can sometimes be a little overwhelming. Massé explains that the wealth of feedback the team has received in Paralives' first few months has been incredibly useful, but cautions that it's "easy to get lost in it," especially as some players want more focus on new content while others want feature improvements. "It can become difficult to decide what to prioritise next," he says.
But Knight says that player feedback has been the most valuable takeaway from Phasmophobia's Early Access period. "It's allowed the game to almost transform into something else," he explains. "By the time we get to 1.0, Phasmophobia is going to be a much bigger and better game."
Endless Early Access
According to GameDiscoverCo, the average Steam Early Access period is 21 months – but some games linger for much longer than that. Massé is hoping Paralives will leave Early Access in 2028, some two years after it launched; but Valheim stayed in Early Access for over five years.
Part of the reason is that the boundaries kept changing. Svensson says he started Valheim as a solo project, but released it into Early Access in February 2021 as he "couldn't afford to keep working on it," and Early Access seemed like "the only reasonable solution at the time." In the first month, it sold more than five million copies; by 2022, over 10 million. Valheim 1.0 was finally released on September 9, 2026, by which time it had sold 17 million copies.
"The original plan was perhaps two or three years in Early Access, but with every update our ambitions have only increased," Svensson explains. members.title: Stardew Valley-Style Dark Fantasy RPG Delays Steam Early Access Launch to 2027

news.body:
Stardew Valley-Style Dark Fantasy RPG Delays Steam Early Access Launch to 2027
The development team behind Emberville said they need more time to add changes and improvements.
Cygnus Cross, the developer of the upcoming pixel action RPG Emberville, frequently described as "Stardew Valley meets Diablo," has delayed the game's Early Access release to January 7, 2027.
Emberville was originally set to launch in Early Access on October 27. The developers shared on Steam that they made the call after "extensive discussions," and thanked the players for understanding and patience.
They need extra time to include the changes and enhancements to make the game "the best it can be"; for example, reworking bow combat would take more time than they had. The January release is meant to define the game's core mechanics and show where it is headed through Early Access.
Read the social media announcement below:
"An update on Early Access:
The Cygnus Cross team has made the difficult decision to delay the Emberville release to January 7, 2027. This decision wasn't made lightly. After a fantastic Steam Next Fest, we realized we simply needed more time to include all the changes and improvements that we think will make the game the best it can be.
Thank you for playing our Steam Next Fest demo, and for all the wonderful comments, suggestions, and feedback. Look forward to our Early Access release in January!
Cygnus Cross"
Cygnus Cross
Emberville combines Stardew Valley's pixel art style with dark-fantasy elements and is set in the vast, magical underground world of Vitromotus, which players must escape. The game features action-focused combat rewarding positioning and timing with weapon-bound combos, exploration, uncovering the locals' stories, and making choices.
Cygnus Cross
The pixel RPG has a star-studded voice cast, featuring Matthew Mercer (Critical Role, Baldur's Gate 3, Overwatch), Jennifer English (Baldur's Gate 3, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33), Ben Starr (Final Fantasy XVI, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33), Nick Apostolides (Resident Evil 2 and 4, Dead Space), Elias Toufexis (Deus Ex, Starfield), and many other popular voice actors.

news.body:
10月24日至25日，由成都日蚀边缘工作室（Eclipse Glow Games）研发并发行的单机动作冒险游戏《湮灭之潮》亮相核聚变试玩会。在约一小时的试玩中，玩家得以体验制作组在科隆、成都试玩版本基础上进一步打磨的游戏内容，感受游戏的阶段性优化。
本次试玩中，主角格雯德琳的面部呈现是重点优化之一。在沿用原有面部模型的基础上，制作组进一步调整了角色的灯光与渲染效果改善部分场景与镜头下的光照表现。此外，本次版本也修复了部分已知问题，进一步完善试玩体验。
试玩会前夕，10月23日，《湮灭之潮》游戏监制陈琦与游戏主策练鹏飞做客「核电波」，首次通过深度访谈，分享作品的创作理念、研发历程，以及主角格雯德琳的塑造过程，并回应玩家对角色面部等问题的关注。
针对玩家关心的格雯面部变化，两位主创在访谈中解释，格雯始终沿用同一套面部模型，从未更换；不同阶段呈现出的观感差异，则与灯光、材质、面部绑定技术等因素有关。本次核聚变试玩版本也针对玩家反馈，通过灯光和渲染的调整，改善了脸部视觉表现。
制作人与音乐总监同台，揭秘《湮灭之潮》音乐与美术设计巧思
10月25日，《湮灭之潮》制作人付坤与音乐总监薄彩生登上核聚变舞台，结合现场策划的实机演示，分享游戏音乐与角色设计背后的创作思路。曾参与《影之刃零》音乐创作的薄彩生，也讲述了他如何通过音乐塑造角色、传递情绪。这场结合实机演示的舞台分享，让玩家得以进一步了解游戏体验背后的创作考量。
《湮灭之潮》是一款日蚀边缘工作室研发并发行的国产单机买断制骑士幻想动作冒险游戏，游戏基于虚幻 5 引擎打造，仅登录 PC 及主机平台，游戏以「异世界入侵下的破碎伦敦」为核心设定，玩家将扮演灾难中的幸存者格雯德琳（Gwendolyn），在现实与幻境交织的伦敦废墟中展开冒险，对抗由异世界而来的威胁，并逐步揭开世界倾覆背后的秘密。
《湮灭之潮》现正面向 PC（Steam 与 Epic Games Store）、Xbox Series X|S 及 PlayStation5 平台开发中。
日蚀边缘工作室（Eclipse Glow Games）是一家面向全球玩家开发及发行 PC 和主机游戏的工作室，总部位于四川成都。工作室当前正在开发基于亚瑟王神话的动作冒险游戏《湮灭之潮》，团队由 150 余名开发者组成，成员曾参与《如龙》（Yakuza）《荣耀战魂》（For Honor）《刺客信条》（Assassin's Creed）《女神异闻录》（Persona）与《波斯王子》（Prince of Persia）等知名游戏的研发。

members.title: 梁其伟长文致谢玩家，《影之刃零》明日上线！
《影之刃零》倒计时2天，系列人气角色虚空高清海报公布
从《影之刃零》完整版中能看到的，是审美、技术与匠心
《影之刃零》PC版现已开启预下载
江湖大幕将启！国产3A《影之刃零》29日发售，上咪咕游戏先人一步入局

news.body:
国产3A武侠动作游戏《影之刃零》上线在即，距离游戏解锁仅剩不到20小时。制作人梁其伟在个人微博发布长文，回顾了从《雨血》诞生至今，跨越二十年的创作历程，以及《影之刃零》多年的研发幕后故事。
对梁其伟来说，《影之刃零》的源头，要追溯到二十年前。求学阶段，他用RPG Maker 制作的独立游戏《雨血：死镇》，以传统武侠为基底，融入人体改造、平行世界等构想，搭建起 “影境” 的世界观雏形。当初只是求学期间的精神寄托，最终一步步演变成贯穿他整个职业生涯的重要作品。
三年多前，灵游坊带着尚不成熟的《影之刃零》首支预告登上 PlayStation 发布会。彼时工作室体量不大，影之刃 IP 对于全球玩家而言也相对陌生。发布会之后，团队暂停其他在研项目，集中全部资源投入本作，打磨内容品质。团队完成数千小时动作捕捉，走访国内城乡开展实地 3D 扫描；同时邀请舞狮、峨眉剑术、少林拳法相关的武术大师担任动作指导。由动作导演羊柳带队的动捕团队，在甄子丹的顾问共创之下，设计了整套攻击、格挡、闪避、连招与处决动作。
梁其伟提到，《影之刃零》并不打算做成门槛很高的硬核作品。游戏玩法上手直观，操作感受贴近玩家熟悉的动作游戏逻辑。团队重新复盘 ARPG 多年来的设计思路，对经典玩法进行重组，兼顾普通玩家的游玩体验，同时为偏爱高难度挑战的玩家保留足够的战斗爽感。
开发期间，团队在海内外多场展会收集玩家反馈，在很多细微之处持续优化：玩家可自由调整刀剑碰撞音效，自定义拼刀的听觉感受；PS5 版本提供三套预设键位，PC 端支持完全自定义按键；游戏也完成多规格屏幕适配，覆盖显示器、掌机乃至 3:1 以上的超宽显示器。
但技术之外，梁其伟认为成就这款作品的，是团队骨子里的一份执着与热忱。游戏内数场关键战斗关卡由 00 后团队成员主导完成；绝大部分角色、场景设定图由美术 Michael 独立绘制；配乐薄彩生（阿薄）独自完成超十小时游戏原声，包揽作曲、演奏、混音，还参与了游戏音频控制系统的落地。
开发路上，梁其伟曾多次做出 “令人窒息的决定”：推翻已经完工、质量尚可的内容，选择重构甚至直接舍弃，但依靠团队的理解与坚持，他们依然把全部想法与创意倾注进游戏之中。在他的构想里，《影之刃零》核心是让玩家真切感受到强大与炫酷。这种力量不靠旁白文字灌输，而是来自每一次挥刀、格挡、闪避和处决。强敌压迫感、压抑的江湖故事，还有主角仅剩六十六天生命的设定，最终都是为了让玩家在战斗中，体会到这份由外到内的强大。
从早年RPG Maker引擎制作的独立作品，到面向全球推出的国产3A武侠大作，《影之刃零》承载着梁其伟二十年的创作轨迹，同时，《影之刃零》也是这群热爱游戏的开发者们，送给所有玩家的一份真诚礼物。
20年前，我在学校开始制作自己的第一部独立游戏《雨血：死镇》。在这款用 RPG Maker 制作的业余游戏里，我用稚嫩的技术构建了一个心目中的幻想世界：一个以中国传统武侠为根基，又融入人体改造、平行世界等元素的”影境“。
那时的我，并不知道未来的人生与职业会走向何方。制作游戏原本只是我在求学期间的精神寄托，却在不知不觉中，成为了我生命中最重要的一部分。
3年多以前，当带着第一版还相当粗糙的《影之刃零》预告片登上PlayStation的发布会时，我们看起来像是个有点胆大妄为，贸然把半成品曝光在全球观众的审视下的新工作室。“影之刃”也只是又一个原创IP，其中的世界，人物，故事对大多数人来说是完全陌生的。
我们砍掉了其它在研项目，不断拓展制作规模、提升作品精度，并倾尽所能，汇聚技术、经验、资源与各方协助：数千小时的动作捕捉，遍访中国城镇与山村进行的 3D 扫描，由广东舞狮大师指导的舞狮、由峨眉剑术大师指导的剑阵、由少林寺僧人指导的拳法。除此之外，我们还组建了一只高效，专业的武打动捕团队，由动作导演羊柳带领，并在我们的偶像——甄子丹的顾问下，为游戏制作了不计其数的攻击，防御，躲闪，连招，处决动作……
关于《影之刃零》，你可能已经看到了许多的评测，但实际上你可能又不需要看太多。明天进入游戏后，你会发现一切玩法都显得自然，简单，熟悉，但我们把这些熟悉的玩法重新创作了一遍，并将它们组合成了一个新的整体——几年来，我们深度思考了整个ARPG及动作游戏的许多“祖宗之法”，研究究竟什么是玩家最想要的元素，以及如何将这些元素组合起来达成我们的目的——让所有喜爱武侠文化，喜欢动作表现的玩家都乐在其中。毕竟这是一款游戏，它存在的目的是为了让大部分人感到好玩，放松和享受，同时给那些追求挑战的玩家热血沸腾的额外刺激。
在研发的几年中，我们在各种展会，试玩会上与大量普通玩家进行交流，从国内的北京到上海，从美国洛杉矶到巴西圣保罗……我们体会到玩家的需求，并在一些细枝末节的地方同样争取做好：
譬如，我们的音频设置中拥有“刀剑碰撞音色”调节选项，玩家可以自主设置拼刀时的感受；我们的PS5版中拥有三种不同的键位布局（PC版则可更灵活地自由设置）；另外，我们对主流的屏幕比例都进行了适配，包括16:9的显示器，电视，16:10的笔记本，掌机，还有超过3:1的超宽屏幕等。
但是研发不总是那么理性的，那些感性和疯狂的元素也许铸就了游戏中最“美味”的部分。我们的几场重要的战斗，都由几位年轻的00后同事完成；我们全部的角色和大部分的场景设定，由Michael一个人全部画完；更不用说“无法无天”的阿薄了——他独自完成了超过10小时的音乐素材，除了部分特殊乐器和演唱外，他做了全部工作，包括作曲，演奏，混音，还指导完成了游戏内的播放控制，音量控制等。
在进行了多年的研发后，我觉得“技术”和“经验”已经是无需讨论的基础话题，我最关注的，反而是大家的“精神状态”，是否在超越了技术和经验后，藏着某种“癫”和“痴”——武侠游戏做着做着，我们自己似乎也成为了武侠中的那种人物。
在这几年中，我没少对团队说的一句话是“今天我要宣布一个令人窒息的决定”，这往往意味着把某些大家按部就班做完，但已经打造精良的东西拆掉，重构，甚至彻底放弃，同时也意味着大量的返工，或把包含大量工作量的内容直接舍弃，感谢团队的支持和理解，我们做到了！我们已经将所有的思考和创造力，灌注在这部作品之中。
《影之刃零》的存在，是为了让你感觉到自身的强大和炫酷，无论任何敌人出现在你的面前，你最终会将他们击败。这种感受不是通过简单的“告知”实现的，而是通过你挥出去的每一刀，每次格挡，每个闪避，以及那眼花缭乱的暴力美学处决来体现的；敌人的强大也是为了衬托你自身的强大，乃至那看起来黑暗，略显悲剧的背景故事——六十六天生命倒计时，也是为了让这种强大由外在而拓展到内心。
现在，我们郑重邀请你体验《影之刃零》。它一方面源自我当年求学时在困苦与迷茫中创作的那部独立游戏；但它也凝聚了我们在能力所及之内所能倾注的一切。
这是一部以炽热的心打造的，具有庞大体量的作品。这是一小群热爱游戏的人（只不过恰巧也是开发者），献给所有热爱游戏的人的礼物。
我们赶在发售前准备了一个首日补丁，大约5G大小，可以极大提升光线追踪和路径追踪的性能，以及部分bug修复。如果你在此前完成了预下载，可以在启动游戏前进一步更新补丁后再开始游戏，如果没有预下载，那么直接下载的就是最新版本。
我们花费了大量时间用于提升光栅化的美术表现，即使关闭光线追踪，仍然可以完美传达场景的美术设计风格。中低端机器乃至于掌机的体验也经过了大量测试，值得大家尝试。
我们发现Nvidia最新的621.01驱动存在部分不稳定的性能表现，经过测试，617.42 驱动是目前适配《影之刃零》最为理想的驱动版本。如果已经更新到617.42之后的版本，可以将驱动回退至617.42，选择清洁安装，并等待Nvidia的新一版驱动更新（相信他们很快就会发布）。

members.title: Warhorse Studios hit by an undetailed cybersecurity incident
Warhorse Studios hit by cyberattack, company systems and data affected

news.body:
Warhorse Studios hit by an undetailed cybersecurity incident
The developer behind the Kingdom Come: Deliverance games has revealed that it has been hit by a 'serious' cybersecurity attack and is taking steps to assess the full impact.
Kingdom Come: Deliverance and Unnamed Lord of the Rings RPG developer Warhorse Studios announced today on its website that the studio has been a victim of a noteworthy cyberattack, the full scope of which was not detailed or fully assessed yet. The post does, however, confirm that the attack provided unauthorized access to company systems and data.
"This is a serious incident for Warhorse Studios and everyone affected," writes Warhorse CEO Martin Frývaldský. "Our immediate priority is to secure our systems, establish the full extent of the breach, and take the necessary steps to protect our employees, partners, and community. We are dedicating the resources needed to address this situation and will communicate further information as soon as we responsibly can.”
The studio confirms in the update that it is working with cybersecurity experts to get a handle on the attack. The studio is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Fellowship Entertainment, a spin-off of Embracer.
When a studio is the victim of a cyberattack, the data the hackers obtain can have numerous cascading effects on the company and its employees. Payroll data, including social security numbers or international equivalents, can be exposed and published online. If the hackers are able to access internal files, projects currently being worked on can also be exposed.
One such example is when Pokémon developer Game Freak suffered an attack in 2024 that exposed the data of 2600 employees. The hack also led to the public release of development information of assets, concept art, and unannounced game development plans.
It's unknown at this time if the attack on Warhorse achieved a similar scale.

news.title: Sucker Punch lays off 24 to align with 'current market', 'next project needs'
news.summary_raw: 24 members of staff have been laid off from the studio making for an estimated total staff reduction of around 10 percent.

members.title: Sucker Punch lays off 24 to align with 'current market', 'next project needs'
Sucker Punch Productions reportedly lays off 24 employees following launch of Ghost of Yōtei: Complete Edition

news.body:
Ghost of Yotei developer Sucker Punch has laid off two dozen employees, a reduction made both amid ongoing market turbulence and as the studio looks toward development of its next project.The report, first detailed by Aftermath and later confirmed by Sucker Punch, discloses that 24 members of staff have been laid off from the studio, making for a total staff reduction of around 10 percent according to Aftermath’s estimated numbers.
An email sent to staff said that the layoffs were a both a reaction to ongoing market challenges and were necessary to better align the team to the needs of Sucker Punch’s next project.
“After carefully observing the challenges in the market and reviewing the team needs for our next project, we’ve decided to make some staffing reductions,” reads the email shared by Aftermath. “Several positions across Sucker Punch will be eliminated as a result.”

news.title: How does terrain work in video games?
news.summary_raw: A beginner’s guide to video game terrain: how tiles, heightmaps, voxels, and noise create the ground players walk on, and how to design terrain.

members.title: How does terrain work in video games?

news.body:
How does terrain work in video games?
Unity Team - Unity Technologies
A beginner’s guide to video game terrain: how tiles, heightmaps, voxels, and noise create the ground players walk on, and how to design terrain that’s fun to explore.
Rolling hills, jagged mountains, sandy beaches, winding rivers. When you explore a game world, the ground under your feet does a lot of quiet work. It sets the mood, shapes where you can go, and decides what you see on the horizon. But what is that ground actually made of?
This guide explains how game terrain works, from tile-based 2D maps to 3D landscapes, in plain language. You’ll learn the main techniques game makers use, how terrain gets its look, how worlds can be generated automatically, and how to design terrain that’s fun to move through.
What is terrain in video games?
Video game terrain is the ground surface of a game world. That means it’s the main surface that players and other moving objects travel across, and the base that everything else sits on. It usually imitates natural surfaces like rock, sand, gravel, and soil, but it can also stand in for human-made ground like cracked pavement or overgrown paving stones.
Terrain isn’t just scenery. Shaping the land is a design tool. One level design reference defines landscape design in games as the purposeful shaping of the land to support how players move and what you want them to experience.
Terrain in 2D games: tiles
Many 2D games build their worlds out of tiles: small, regular images that fit together like a grid to form the whole level. A single grass tile, a dirt tile, and a water tile can be reused over and over to build a large map. Tiles can define how a world looks, how it works – which squares are walkable, which are walls – or both.
Tiles are a natural fit for top-down and side-view games, and for anyone who wants to build levels quickly from a small set of reusable pieces.
Terrain in 3D games: heightmaps
Most 3D terrain starts with a heightmap. A heightmap is a grayscale image where each pixel’s brightness represents height: white is high, black is low, and gray is somewhere in between. The game takes a flat grid and raises or lowers each point based on the matching pixel, turning a flat sheet into hills and valleys.
Heightmaps are efficient and easy to edit, which is why they’re so common. But they have one big limitation: each point on the map can only have one height. That means a heightmap can’t represent caves, tunnels, or overhangs – anything where ground sits above other ground.
Beyond heightmaps: voxels
For worlds that need caves or terrain that can be dug and destroyed, some games use voxels instead. A voxel system treats the world as a 3D grid of tiny cells, each either solid or empty. This makes caves, overhangs, floating islands, and fully destructible ground possible. Historically, the trade-off has been complexity: voxel terrain is harder to build and run, so it’s usually used only when those abilities are essential to the game. However, this is starting to change, as AI tools like Unity Spark begin to make these approaches more accessible.
How terrain gets its look
Shape is only half the story. Terrain also needs surfaces: grass on the plains, rock on the cliffs, sand by the water.
A common technique is the splatmap: a hidden texture that tells the game which surface to show where, and how to blend between them. A splatmap often has four color channels, each assigned to a different material – for example, grass, soil, rock, and sand. Where the grass channel is strong, you see grass. Where two channels overlap, the surfaces blend smoothly instead of switching abruptly.
Surfaces don’t always have to be painted by hand. Many tools apply materials automatically using rules based on the terrain itself – for example, putting rock on steep slopes. Some go further and decorate whole regions automatically with themed sets of plants, rocks, and textures, often called biomes.
Generating terrain automatically
Some games create their terrain with code instead of by hand. This is called procedural generation, and one of the most common starting points is noise.
Noise, in this sense, is a mathematical pattern of smooth, random-looking values. Treat those values as heights and you get a heightmap of gentle hills. Layering several versions of the noise at different scales – big hills plus smaller bumps – produces more natural, rugged terrain. From there, you can turn the lowest areas into water, and combine height with a second noise pattern for moisture to decide where forests, deserts, and snow appear.
Because each point can be calculated on its own, this approach can even generate worlds that seem to go on forever, creating each area only when the player gets close.
Noise has limits, though. Different areas don’t relate to each other, so the map can start to feel samey, and it usually takes a lot of tweaking to get results you like. It’s a great, quick starting point for small projects and game jams, which many creators later replace with something more tailored to their game.
Designing terrain that’s fun to explore
Good terrain isn’t just realistic. It supports how players move. A few principles from level design help:
Plan the big picture first.
Start with a simple map that labels the main areas and how they connect. Then shape rough hills, valleys, and paths before adding any detail. Resist the urge to sculpt fine details early.
Decide on scale early.
How far apart should places be? How steep can a slope be before it’s too steep to climb? Work this out early, because most terrain tools make it hard to move or resize big landforms later. Moving a mountain is harder than moving a wall.
Make it readable.
Players should be able to tell where they can and can’t go. Watch out for slopes that look climbable but aren’t, and spots where players can get stuck. Leave generous flat space at the top and bottom of ramps so players don’t overshoot and fall.
Borrow from nature.
Water flows downhill and curves around obstacles, so rivers – and the valleys around them – tend to curve. People follow the land, so paths usually curve around hills and trees too. Trees work like walls you can walk through, enclosing spaces without fully blocking them.
Test it by playing it.
Walk through your terrain often. Look for areas that feel too big, routes that feel too long, and places where players can get stuck or fall into a gap.
Terrain techniques at a glance
Build worlds worth exploring
Terrain is more than background. It decides where players go, what they see, and how the world feels. Pick the technique that fits your game, plan the big shapes before the details, and keep testing whether the ground you’ve built is fun to move through.

news.title: Frame rate explained: What is fps in video games?
news.summary_raw: Learn what frames per second (fps) means, why 30, 60, and 120 fps are common targets, why steady beats fast, and how to pick a frame rate for your video game.

members.title: Frame rate explained: What is fps in video games?

news.body:
Frame rate explained: What is fps in video games?
Unity Team - Unity Technologies
Frame rate is how many individual images (frames) a video game draws and displays per second, measured in frames per second (fps). Each frame is a snapshot of the game world. Shown in rapid succession, they create the illusion of motion. Keep reading to learn about fps benchmarking, why 30, 60, and 120 fps are common targets, why steady beats fast, and how to pick a frame rate for your video game.
What is frame rate in video games?
A video game can be likened to a flipbook. Many times a second, it draws a fresh picture of the world – where the character is, where the enemies are, what the light looks like – and puts it on screen. Do that fast and steadily enough and your brain stops seeing pictures and starts seeing motion.
How fast and how steadily that happens is called frame rate. It’s one of the most talked-about numbers in games, and one of the most misunderstood. This guide explains what it means, which numbers matter, and how to choose the right target for the game you want to make.
What frame rate means
Each picture a game draws is called a frame. Frame rate is how many frames the game draws every second, measured in frames per second (fps). A game running at 30 fps shows 30 new pictures each second; at 60 fps, it shows 60.
More frames per second generally means smoother motion, because each picture is a smaller step from the one before. That smoothness also makes a game feel more responsive, since what you see catches up to what you pressed sooner.
What is frame time?
Frame time is how long it takes to render a single frame, measured in milliseconds (ms). It’s the inverse of frame rate: 1000 ms divided by fps:
Developers often find frame time more useful than frame rate. Think of it as a budget. At 60 fps, everything the game needs to do – move characters, check collisions, run the rules, draw the scene – has to fit inside roughly 16.7 ms. If one frame needs more, it’s late, and the player sees it.
Frame rate vs refresh rate
Your game determines how many frames it makes. The screen decides how often it can show a new one. That second number is the display’s refresh rate, measured in hertz (Hz).
The two need to line up. A screen that refreshes 60 times a second can’t show more than 60 new frames per second, so a 120 fps target only pays off on a display that refreshes at 120 Hz. And when the frame rate doesn’t divide evenly into the refresh rate, frames can end up on screen for uneven lengths of time, which looks like stutter even when the average number seems fine.
That’s why some targets that look odd make sense. A 40 fps mode works well on a 120 Hz screen because 40 divides evenly into 120 – each frame stays up for exactly three refreshes.
Common frame rate targets and what they’re for
There’s no single “right” frame rate. Each common target is a trade-off between smoothness and how much the game can draw each frame.
A few patterns stand out:
- Many console games let players choose. A quality mode might run at 30 fps with sharper visuals, while a performance mode runs at 60 fps with lower resolution or fewer effects.
- Fast, precise games lean hard toward 60 fps. Fighting games, for example, are often locked to 60 fps because the timing of every attack animation is counted in frames.
- VR is stricter. In a headset, a low or unsteady frame rate is more than an annoyance – it can contribute to motion sickness, which is why VR platforms set firm minimums.
Why steady beats fast
Here’s the part that surprises most new creators: a consistent frame rate often feels better than a higher one that keeps changing. A steady 30 fps can feel smoother than a 60 fps that keeps dipping.
The reason is that players notice change more than they notice the number. When most frames arrive on time and a few arrive late, those late frames show up as hitches, stutters, or brief freezes – even if the average frame rate looks great.
That’s also why the average alone can mislead you. One way to judge consistency is to look at your slowest frames, not just the typical ones. Imagine three games, each measured over the same stretch of play:
The “unstable” game has the same average as the “smooth” one, but players would describe them very differently. Sudden freezes like these often come from work that happens all at once mid-game, such as preparing new visual effects the first time they appear or loading new content while the player moves through the world.
Locked vs unlocked frame rates
This is why many games lock or cap their frame rate. A locked frame rate holds the game at a fixed number, like 30 or 60, even if the hardware could sometimes go faster. An unlocked frame rate lets it run as fast as it can, which means it rises and falls with what’s on screen.
Unlocked frame rates can look uneven and can cause screen tearing, where parts of two different frames show at once. Displays that support variable refresh rate (VRR) adjust to the game’s output and smooth much of this out. If you’re not sure which to choose, locking to a target you can reliably hit is usually the safer starting point.
What lowers a game’s frame rate
Every frame has to fit inside its time budget. When it doesn’t, the frame rate drops. The work generally falls into two buckets:
- Game logic: everything the game thinks about, such as character behavior, physics, and rules. Too many objects doing too much at once can slow things down.
- Drawing the scene: everything the game shows, such as the number of objects on screen, the complexity of their materials and effects, and the resolution.
Knowing which bucket is the problem matters, because the fixes are different. Lowering the resolution won’t help much if the slowdown comes from hundreds of characters making decisions at once.
This is also why games offer trade-offs. To hold 60 fps, a game might lower its resolution, reduce effects, or use dynamic resolution, which quietly lowers the resolution during busy moments so the frame rate stays steady. On slower devices, lowering graphics settings is one of the most direct ways to recover a heavy, sluggish frame rate.
Frame rate on phones and battery
On mobile, frame rate affects more than smoothness. Drawing frames the player won’t benefit from uses power. Running at a frame rate that matches the screen and avoiding unnecessary screen updates can help battery life. Many phones support several refresh rates, such as 120, 90, 60, and 30 Hz, so a game can pick the one that fits.
For a slower-paced mobile game, a lower, steady frame rate can be a reasonable choice. For a fast action game, the smoothness of a higher frame rate is usually worth the power.
How to choose a frame rate for your video game
To choose a frame rate for your video game, ask yourself these questions:
- How fast is the action? Fast, reaction-based games – action, racing, rhythm, fighting – benefit most from 60 fps or higher. Slower, more deliberate games can feel fine at 30 fps, as long as it’s steady.
- Where will people play? Check the platform’s typical screens. A 120 fps target only matters on a 120 Hz display, and VR platforms may set minimums you have to meet.
- What matters more – detail or responsiveness? If your game is about atmosphere and rich visuals, a steady 30 fps can free up budget. If it’s about precise control, protect the frame rate first.
- Can you hold it everywhere? Test the busiest moment in your game – the biggest fight, the most crowded scene – not just the quiet ones. That’s where the frame rate will dip first.
- Do you need options? Offering a quality mode and a performance mode lets players choose their own trade-off.
A quick frame rate checklist
Before you share your game, run through this list:
- I’ve picked a target frame rate and know why.
- My game holds that target in its busiest moments, not just on average.
- I’ve checked for sudden freezes, especially the first time new areas or effects appear.
- My target fits the screens my players will use.
- If I’m making a VR game, I meet the platform’s minimum frame rate.
- On mobile, I’m not drawing more frames than the game needs.
Keep it smooth, keep it steady
Frame rate isn’t a score to max out. It’s a promise to the player that the game will respond the same way every time they press a button. Pick a target that suits your game, protect it in the busiest moments, and remember that steady almost always beats fast.

news.title: 10 things you need to know before building your first video game
news.summary_raw: New to video game making? Learn the 10 design decisions to plan before you build – from core loop and scope to physics, camera, controls, and playtesting.

members.title: 10 things you need to know before building your first video game

news.body:
10 things you need to know before building your first video game
Unity Team - Unity Technologies
You’ve got an idea for a video game. Maybe it’s a puzzle you keep solving in your head, or a world you’ve been sketching for years. What you might not have is a background in code, art, or game engines.
Cutting out the code doesn’t cut out the design work. Every game still needs dozens of decisions: how things move, what the player sees, and what happens when they press a button. You’ll still make every one of them – just as a designer, not a programmer, describing what you want instead of coding it.
Here are 10 things to think through before you start building your first video game.
1. Know what your player does, again and again
Every game has a core loop: a repeatable sequence of actions, often shaped like challenge, action, and reward. Before you think about levels, characters, or upgrades, get that loop right. The question that matters most at this stage is “is this game fun?” – and piling on polish can end up band-aiding over the problem that the core game isn’t fun.
Try this: Describe what your player does in one sentence.
2. Pick a genre and learn what players expect
A genre is the type of game you’re making – puzzle, racing, platformer, and so on – and each one comes with expectations. Take platformers. Players expect levels with uneven ground and floating platforms that they cross by jumping and climbing. A platformer without jumping would feel wrong to most players.
Building on something players already know helps them pick up your game faster. A familiar foundation lets a game ramp up rapidly without alienating the player. The same goes for controls: When they match what players expect, the experience feels frictionless. But you don’t have to copy everything. Many new games stand out by changing just one thing: making it easier or harder, or adding or taking away a control. So learn what players expect from your genre, then pick the one thing you’ll do differently.
3. Keep your scope small enough to finish
Ambition is great. Finishing is better. Be ruthless about the game’s scope, and when you’re torn between options, ask which choice is going to take the least amount of time.
Test ideas with quick prototypes. A prototype lets you answer a question, quickly, so keep your prototypes small and specific. Just don’t get stuck there: If you never stop making prototypes, you won’t make a video game.
4. Choose a visual style you can sustain
There’s no single right look. There’s no such thing as the “best game art style” since it depends on your idea, your resources, your intended audience, the desired game play, and more.
Start with feeling. Ask “What are we trying to convey? What should the player feel?” Teams often explore this through mood pieces, concept art and sketches before production begins. Then stay consistent – find a sweet spot between variety and cohesion. If you’re going for pixel art, for example, a limited palette helps unify your visuals.
5. Decide where the camera sits
Your camera choice affects controls, level design, art and how the game feels. First-person views are immersive, but players can’t see their character. Top-down views give a clear layout with less sense of height. Isometric views feel 3D, but depth can be hard to judge.
How much the camera can see – its field of view – shapes mood, too. A narrow view feels much more claustrophobic, while a wider one gives much more peripheral vision. Decide what your player needs to see, and what you want them to feel.
6. Plan your physics – even if it isn’t realistic
Physics is just the rules for how things move in your game. How high can your character jump? How fast do they fall? What happens when they run into a wall? You won’t need any math, but you will need to decide.
Your game doesn’t have to work like the real world. Real-world physics doesn’t always improve the experience. What matters is that your rules stay the same every time, because results that don’t make sense frustrate players. Lots of games bend the rules on purpose. In many platformers, you can still jump for a moment after running off a ledge.
Before you build, ask yourself:
- What can bump into what?
- Should your character feel light and floaty, or heavy and solid?
- Where will you bend the rules to make the game more fun?
7. Make controls feel responsive
When a player presses a button, the game should answer right away. In a study of 94 players, added delays of half a second and one second significantly increased player frustration while significantly decreasing enjoyment and immersion. A useful target is to keep the gap between action and response faster than 100 milliseconds (0.1 second) whenever possible.
Think about the device, too. Touchscreens offer little physical feedback, so touch controls should be forgiving and designed for fluidity, rather than precision.
8. Give every action feedback
Every action needs a response the player can see or hear. Game makers call this “juice”: the little flashes, shakes, and sounds that make an action feel satisfying. Research on how games feel has focused on exactly this – controls that respond quickly, and feedback that’s a little exaggerated.
Juice doesn’t have to be fancy. In one study, players liked comic-style sound words popping up onscreen, like “POW” or “BOOM,” about as much as bursts of sparks and debris.
Sound matters as much as visuals. It only takes a few seconds of playing your favorite game on mute to realize how important sound is. What’s on your screen counts as feedback too. A head-up display (HUD) – the health bar, score, or timer – needs as much planning as the rest of your game. Many games end up with weak on-screen displays because they’re treated as an afterthought.
9. Design the challenge, and how players win or lose
Every game needs a way to win, a way to lose, and a path between them. Difficulty is a careful balancing act, and a game that feels fair can keep players in that challenge zone for a long time. When players fail, they should know why. The worst case is a player who fails and has no idea what they did wrong or how to improve.
Difficulty is really subjective, so consider offering presets – ideally four or more according to Xbox – that players can change at any time without losing game progress. If in doubt, err on the side of easier rather than harder.
10. Playtest early, and design so more people can play
You can’t see your own game with fresh eyes, so let other people play it. Friends and family are a great place to start – just try to add a few people who don’t know you, too. Hand them the game, stay quiet, and watch where they hesitate or get stuck. Then fix what you can and test again. Torn between two ideas? Make a quick version of each and let your testers pick the winner.
Plan for accessibility from the start. Xbox estimates there are nearly 450 million players with some form of disability. Accessibility is not about eliminating challenges; it is about adding flexibility to challenges. For controls, that means going beyond simple control remapping – for example, toggles instead of holds and no button mashing.
Start with a plan, then start building
You don’t need every answer before you begin. But one page that covers your core loop, genre, scope, style, camera, physics, controls, feedback, challenge, and testing plan will save you a lot of rework later. Keep it short, keep it honest, and update it as you learn.

上海，2026年10月28日 —— 全球领先的游戏开发公司维塔士（Virtuos）宣布，正式获选加入虚幻引擎服务合作伙伴计划（Unreal Engine Service Partner Program），成为该计划落地大中华区后首批公布的六家服务合作伙伴之一。相关合作伙伴身份已于10月22-23日举办的Unreal Fest Shanghai 2026上正式揭晓。入选该计划意味着维塔士通过了 Epic Games 对服务合作伙伴的严格审核，也进一步印证了维塔士在 Unreal Engine 项目实践、技术能力与专业服务方面的综合实力。
随着游戏品质要求持续提升、开发规模不断扩大，开发团队需要同时应对内容生产效率、技术复杂度、跨平台开发及交付节奏等多重挑战。自2004年成立以来，维塔士持续与全球开发商和发行商合作，在不同类型和规模的游戏项目中积累开发与制作经验，并长期参与 Unreal Engine 项目的开发实践。在游戏开发、美术制作及技术优化等全流程服务中，维塔士持续深化 Unreal Engine 相关能力，并依托全球资源与本地团队的协同优势，为开发团队提供灵活、专业且贴近项目实际需求的支持。
对于此次成功入选，维塔士中国区总经理田立表示：“对游戏开发者而言，优秀的引擎不仅是技术工具，更是将创意转化为现实的重要伙伴。在此，我们向 Epic Games 团队表示诚挚感谢。成为虚幻引擎大中华区服务合作伙伴，是对维塔士过往项目实践的认可，也为我们开启了全新的合作契机。未来，我们将持续加码 Unreal Engine 的人才培养与技术探索，以更成熟、灵活和高效的方式赋能合作伙伴。我们期待与 Epic Games 及 Unreal 社区携手前行，共同创造更多卓越的游戏体验。”
此次加入虚幻引擎服务合作伙伴计划，为维塔士在大中华区进一步深化Unreal Engine相关能力建设及生态合作开启了新的机会。未来，维塔士也将与更多开发者和行业伙伴分享项目经验、探索技术创新，共同推动高品质游戏内容与体验的发展。
关于维塔士
维塔士（Virtuos）成立于2004年，是全球最大的游戏开发公司之一。公司总部位于新加坡，在亚洲、欧洲和北美均设有工作室及办事处。维塔士专注于全流程游戏开发和美术制作，多年来为超过1,500款主机、PC和移动游戏提供高质量内容，客户覆盖全球前25家游戏公司中的23家。

news.title: Rockstar Games workers to vote on unionization right as Grand Theft Auto VI launches
news.summary_raw: Rockstar employees will have two weeks to decide if they want to recognize the IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union.

members.title: Rockstar Games workers to vote on unionization right as Grand Theft Auto VI launches

news.body:
The Independent Worker's Union of Great Britain has announced that Rockstar Games employees will formally vote on union recognition next month, bringing a years-long union drive to a head and offering employees an opportunity to have a voice on topics like worker pay, overtime, layoffs, flexible working arrangements, and generative AI policies.
Workers will begin voting on November 12, 2026 and will have until November 26 to say "yay" or "nay" to the union. They'll be doing so shortly after Rockstar head of publishing Jennifer Koble commented on the union drive, saying "we go where the team goes. If they want a union, they will have a union."
The vote is taking place independently of an ongoing tribunal over Rockstar's 2025 decision to fire over 30 union employees for "gross misconduct," which the former employees and IWGB have characterized as union busting. Closing arguments for said tribunal will take place on November 17 and 18.
Both of these events land right around the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest entry in the Grand Theft Auto series from Rockstar Games and Take-Two, which releases on November 19. Take-Two says it expects to earn $8 billion in revenue in fiscal year 2027, thanks in part to projected sales of the popular game.
Rockstar Game Workers Union Committee Member acknowledged the timing in a statement accompanying the news, saying that the company's workers have a chance to "make gaming history not once, but twice. As all our hard work, skill and creativity are experienced by GTA VI players for the first time, our voices will now be heard for the first time too."
"For me, this vote comes down to ensuring employees at Rockstar get honesty and openness surrounding the decisions that affect them," Easton-Steel said. "When management choices are kept hidden, we can’t properly address issues like the gender pay gap, the uneven and ever-changing policies on overtime pay, or the concerns many co-workers hold around job security post-release."

members.title: Interview: Konami Envisions Silent Hill Like a Premium TV Series With Various Game Formats

features.body:
Interview: Konami Envisions Silent Hill Like a Premium TV Series With Various Game Formats
Silent Hill Producer Motoi Okamoto and Townfall Director Jon McKellan discuss creative freedom, first-person horror, narrative puzzles, authentic Scottish environments, and the franchise’s future.
In case you missed it
More Silent Hill
Silent Hill’s recent revival has allowed very different development teams to reinterpret the psychological horror series through new countries, characters, mechanics, and perspectives. Rather than connecting every project through a shared storyline, Konami has concentrated on preserving the atmosphere, ambiguity, and deeply personal narratives that define Silent Hill while giving each studio room to establish its own creative identity.
That approach is especially visible in Silent Hill: Townfall, the first full-length entry in the series designed entirely around a first-person perspective. Developed by Screen Burn and released on September 24 for PlayStation 5 and PC, Townfall moves the horror to an isolated Scottish island in 1996, where Simon Ordell must explore an unsettling coastal community, interpret unstable signals through a handheld CRTV, solve story-driven puzzles, and decide when to fight or evade its creatures. Just like Silent Hill 2 Remake and Silent Hill f, it's been well-received.
In this interview, Silent Hill Series Producer Motoi Okamoto and Townfall Director and Writer Jon McKellan explain why Konami avoids imposing a rigid franchise bible on its collaborators, how the series can function more like a collection of premium television stories, and why first-person design allowed Screen Burn to make the town itself the game’s central character.
SILENT HILL: Townfall is set in Scotland in 1996, which immediately gives it a different texture from the series’ more familiar imagery. How did that setting shape the art direction, environment design, atmosphere, and sense of isolation?
Jon McKellan, Silent Hill: Townfall Director and Writer at Screen Burn: The time and place are integral to the experience, and outside of the decision to go first-person with this game, I think they were probably the most important aspects that shaped production. Referencing real coastal towns in Scotland helped us understand how they are shaped—how streets flow into each other, how they radiate outwards from the oldest structures, such as the harbour, and the gradual change in architecture from old to modern.
Setting the game on an island added to the sense of isolation—there’s no escaping your problems, and you can’t just drive away! It allows Simon’s journey to mirror that of the townsfolk: they can’t run away either, and have to face the problems they encounter head-on.
Screen Burn’s previous work has often used technology, interfaces, signals, and fragmented storytelling in very deliberate ways. How did that design language evolve for Townfall, especially when working inside Silent Hill’s tradition of psychological horror, ambiguity, and unreliable perception?
Jon McKellan: The “retro” tech has been part of our DNA since the beginning of Screen Burn, and for me personally, even before that! I think there’s something unpredictable and uncertain about the fuzziness and noise that exist in those old signals compared to the modern day, where everything feels binary. For horror, it’s a perfect match, and there’s a subjectivity to the experience. When squinting to make sense of an image in static, different people might recognize different things, and it’s shaped by their own psyche. It’s just perfect to me, and works really well with the sometimes ambiguous storytelling that permeates Silent Hill as a series.
We wanted to take the “radio static = enemy” concept from previous Silent Hill games further, given our style of storytelling and aesthetics, and that led to the CRTV becoming a core mechanic for the entire game. It allows us to bring in new gameplay elements, but also to tell the story in some different ways, and again lean into that uncertainty. With something like an audio log, it’s often written as though someone is leaving you a message. With the CRTV, the signals can feel disjointed and surreal—like they are trying to tell you something, but it’s not always obvious what.
Townfall is the first Silent Hill psychological horror entry built fully around a first-person perspective. What did first-person allow the team to do differently in terms of fear, intimacy, environmental storytelling, combat, puzzles, and player vulnerability?
Jon McKellan: There were a couple of things we wanted to do that you can only really do in first person, and the CRTV was the main one. Unless we wanted to render that mechanic as a HUD element, which could feel a little too sci-fi, or constantly switch from third to first person and back every time you used it, it would never work well in anything but first person.
Even more important, however, was the sense of space and atmosphere, and making the town the star of the show. In third person, you have to build your environments with a kind of broken scale: doorways have to be larger, room heights much taller than you’d expect, and so on, all to allow the third-person camera to fit comfortably and rotate around the character without bashing into every doorframe or prop in the world. It really changes how you build things and how accurately you can depict the world, especially if you are using “authenticity” as a north star in development.
The result of that decision was that we also got to be much closer to the world itself. In third-person games, when searching cupboards and drawers in a house, you are really just following interact prompts and pressing X when you are told to. You don’t really take in the contents of that drawer, for example. In Townfall, we made searching homes feel much more realistic, and had the player almost subconsciously learn a little about the people who lived there by doing so. It adds so much personality to what is a really standard gameplay mechanic of picking up objects!
The game emphasizes story-driven puzzles that reveal narrative through setup and solutions, rather than only through cinematics. How do you design puzzles that feel mechanically satisfying while also carrying emotional or thematic meaning?
Jon McKellan: It all starts with story for us. The puzzle has to communicate something about the situation or the protagonist’s state of mind before we even begin designing the gameplay inside that puzzle. The Patient chapter is a great example of this, as it’s a puzzle, but not really. It’s really just putting you in someone’s shoes, with no prior knowledge, and asking you to solve the things they have to solve on a daily basis, under pressure.
It feels like a puzzle because you have to figure things out, but really, you are getting to feel the pressure of the situation Zoe was in, and the uncertainty around providing answers puts you right in her mindset on that night too. If we can make the player feel something during a puzzle, rather than just feel clever for solving it, then I think we have something worth pursuing.
The game introduces combat and enemies into Screen Burn’s style of narrative horror, including threats that players may need to fight or evade. How did the team approach creature design, combat pacing, animation, sound, and encounter readability without losing the psychological tension that defines Silent Hill?
Jon McKellan: It’s a tough one, for sure! You are always walking the line between “is this obvious enough?” and “is this too obvious?” and we tried to stay on the understated side of things. We’ve seen some theories about what they represent, and quite often they are sort of the “first glance” interpretation, but there are a lot of subtleties people haven’t picked up on yet, and it’s exciting to see people slowly figure out the layers we’ve buried in there.
For the gameplay side of things, it was a long journey of trying to balance stealth and combat. Being completely underpowered and vulnerable for 12+ hours can be too much, and it was important to give the player a way to level the playing field sometimes. What has been fascinating to see, however, is that even when we hand people a pistol and ammo, they are often too frightened or cautious to use them! They can absolutely take some enemies off the table, but the atmosphere and risk are so intense that they keep hiding and sneaking.
Ultimately, the goal was to give the player options, and that meant combat and stealth were both a little looser than in a dedicated stealth-horror or dedicated action-horror game. Combat is a little more player-initiated, and that can change the pacing massively depending on the type of player. We felt that it was better to give players the freedom to survive their own way, rather than force aggressiveness or force stealth too often.
Can you walk us through the production pipeline for one major environment, puzzle sequence, or enemy encounter, from concept and narrative purpose to level design, art, audio, implementation, testing, and final polish?
Jon McKellan: We’re a very iterative studio at heart—we don’t really set out to design a section, build it, finish it, and move on. We constantly evaluate any section of the game in relation to its neighbouring chapters and the wider game, always zooming out to see how it fits in.
With the “Many Into One” chapter, which is the first “full” Otherworld level under the Medical Centre, it evolved several times. By that point in the game—spoilers!—we know that Simon was treated by Zoe after the accident, but we don’t know much about why or how. So this chapter was designed to illustrate what happened to the other patients that night, and how their deaths ended up benefiting Simon in a way, by using their blood to save him.

本次大会由国际AI泰斗 Kevin Knight 博士领衔开场演讲，发言嘉宾汇聚 OpenAI、Google、阿里、字节、腾讯等全球 AI 科技公司，凝聚一个核心共识：“科技创造增长”产业新周期开启，AI 商业价值必须由真实业务指标验证。

【钛动科技创始人兼CEO李述昊主题演讲】
紧接着，钛动科技创始人兼 CEO 李述昊在其主题分享中，首先将 AI 商业机会落在企业长期、持续投入的营销和销售、编程和产品开发、管理三笔费用上，对应提出 AI for Growth、AI for Innovation与AI for Administration，三者预计构成AI for Work数万亿美元的广阔市场。在这一AI for Work三费框架中，Claude Code等AI产品主攻AI for Innovation，WorkBuddy等AI产品专注协同办公；而钛动科技的Navos Pro则将是AI for Growth的顶尖玩家。

Professional、Proactive、Profitable 三大 Pro 体系背后，有着三层能力供给：
Professional 能力体系融合行业 Know-How 与专属数据，形成数据库、Agent、工作流、互动四大能力：以公域数据、领域Benchmark和垂直场景提供趋势、竞品、选品、素材与投放洞察；以 70+ MCP、100+ Skill 和用户反馈持续调优；以Skill、Template、数字员工，把选品、素材创作、广告诊断等流程标准化、自动化；以意图识别、结果反馈和过程可溯源保障互动。
Proactive 能力体系覆盖日均 10 亿+感知数据、2 亿+感知频次，支持千万+广告诊断、百万+行动建议和 10 万+建议采纳，围绕账户、商品、素材主动监测，输出预算、出价、卖点和素材迭代建议，并联动 Agent 或人工执行。
Profitable 能力体系以“批量创编、规模测试—规模生产、去伪存真—策略迭代、放大收益”推进，通过 Learning Loop 形成结果反馈、策略优化、持续进化闭环。技术底座上，Navos RSI以Agentic RL 驱动 Agent Harness 自迭代，覆盖轨迹采样、奖励设计、策略更新、版本写回与验证。
三层架构由 Agent Harness、32B/27B/5B 专业模型及营销知识库、Benchmark 指标库、方法论资产、多源异构数据和专业样本库构成，支撑多国家、多渠道、多行业、多场景复制。依托上述三大 Pro 体系，Navos 已完整覆盖出海营销链路，同时设置 Navos Lite 和 Navos Pro 双版本矩阵。
【Pro Agent Navos技术架构】
李述昊表示，Agent 演进的本质是工作发起权的转移：Chatbot 阶段，AI 被动应答；Copilot 阶段，AI 辅助执行；到了 Pro-Agent 阶段，AI 开始主动发现业务机会并交付真实增长，Navos Pro 将是这一阶段的代表。
他进一步复盘 Agent 演进故事线之上、更宏观的产业迭代逻辑：2012 年移动互联网时代开启 To C 流量为王的万亿级市场；2018 年 SaaS 时代开启以 To B 为主的万亿级市场；自 2024 年开启的 AI 时代，核心逻辑正从“能力供给”走向“价值验证”。
而钛动科技已通过服务数十万出海品牌的营销实践，率先完成这一“价值验证”，并开启生态布局：2026 年 7 月成为 ChatGPT Ads 全球首批技术合作伙伴，助力品牌 ROI 提升至 2.5 倍；8 月与腾讯 WorkBuddy 达成合作，将模型能力落地海外营销投放场景。
李述昊指出，AI for Growth，只是钛动科技验证 AI 重塑企业生产力的第一步，未来，钛动科技将继续把自身 AI 能力迁移至 AI for Innovation 与 AI for Administration，从而推动企业 AI 生产力的系统性重塑。
OpenAI 商业合作负责人 Lorry Destainville 分享 ChatGPT 商业化前瞻：ChatGPT 每周触达 12 亿用户，OpenAI 正在同步探索 Sponsored Agents和 Visual Ads，特别感谢钛动科技与其联手为品牌主提供可落地、可衡量的AI增长工具。
【大会主持人、钛动科技品牌公关 VP 张羽雪】
【现场圆桌】
随后，由钛动科技品牌公关 VP 张羽雪主持，三场圆桌论坛重磅登场。美国泛大西洋资本周洁、Nextie 创始人李笛、深言序创始人叶军、阿里巴巴千问徐栋同台对话“新兴 AI 技术如何重塑商业未来”；谷歌刘步驰、中金公司赵丽萍、麦芽传媒翁成波、英雄电竞 Josh Ye 共议“ AI 时代的出海大趋势”；BytePlus Terry Wang、阿里巴巴千问邓兆俊、腾讯 WorkBuddy 杨彤对话“ AI 应用商业化的生态实践”。
【钛动科技创始合伙人聂艾玲介绍钛动科技投资版图】
大会最后，钛动科技创始合伙人、生态孵化和战略投资负责人聂艾玲，宣布启动 Pro-Agent Global Challenge 全球挑战赛，面向全球 AI 创业者征集 AI 前沿项目。大赛聚焦 Agent 架构演进、AI 营销、AI 内容入口与算力基础设施等赛道，并将开放资本、产业资源及全球增长通道为项目赋能。
至此，TGC 2026 拼齐了科技创造增长的全景图。AI is Profitable 正在加速兑现，AI for Work 万亿蓝海才刚刚起航。
